headlines.article_text: Dealbook Summit 2026: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Andrew Ross Sorkin speaks onstage during The New York Times DealBook Summit 2025 at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Dec. 3, 2025 in New York City. David Dee Delgado | Getty Images Artificial intelligence, trade tensions, and the need to create trust have been recurring themes at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Andrew Ross Sorkin , founder and editor of DealBook and co-anchor of CNBC's "Squawk Box," has been sitting down in New York with prominent business, economic and political leaders to discuss a wide range of newsmaking issues. The conference comes as OpenAI rival Anthropic is about to make its public debut on Thursday, and it follows a series of widespread tech outages that have grounded airplanes, snarled email, and stymied banking transactions, among other disruptions — a dramatic reminder of society's dependency on these services. In discussing the balancing act that tech leaders are confronting trying to push ahead with AI innovation while attempting to guarantee public safety, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said, "The race dynamic in the fog of war, I think, is a bad thing. I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted." Skydance co-CEO David Ellison emphasized the need to rebuild trust in media organizations. "In a world, you know, where very quickly you're not going to be able to believe your eyes, we think having institutions that earn trust every single day is incredibly important," he said. Meanwhile, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed some frustration over trade relations with the U.S. He said a new deal "should have been done six months ago, but we're not going to sign something that doesn't make sense for Canada." He said he's pressing on in forging other trade partnerships. "We got a lot to do, so we would like to do the deal. But if the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy," he said. "I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it — or maybe it would have been much worse without that," Musk said. He added that if he could he would "rewind the clock" and spend less. "But it certainly shows that you know American elections are not just about money," he said in an interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin. "You know, obviously you can put a lot of money into elections and have an effect that is relatively minor, and I think that that was the case here." —Christina Cheddar Berk 12 Min Ago Musk says Huang is ‘one of the most talented entrepreneurs in history’ watch now VIDEO 3:24 03:24 Elon Musk: No one can really replace Jensen Huang, 'don't think he is disloyal' to the U.S. Fast Money Asked to discuss his view on Nvidia and whether the chipmaker should bring Jensen Huang back as CEO, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk repeated his support for Huang at the Dealbook 2026 Summit, speaking remotely from China on Wednesday. He compared Huang to iconic athlete and Chicago Bulls' champion Michael Jordan at his peak performance, also calling the Nvidia founder, "one of the most talented entrepreneurs in history." "You gotta think long and hard," Musk said, before you kick someone like Jordan off your team in the middle of a winning streak. "There's no one that can really replace Jensen," he added noting how much loyalty Huang commanded at Nvidia, especially among in-demand, engineers who have stayed with the company specifically to work with him. Musk also added that while Huang had "made some mistakes," he doesn't think the Nvidia founder was "disloyal to the United States." Huang reportedly had an affair with a Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, thought to be a possible Chinese spy, before he resigned from Nvidia. —Lora Kolodny 34 Min Ago 'I just want to be in Redmond, Washington,' Nadella says Just before leaving the stage, Microsoft's Nadella was asked about why he has tended to shy away from gatherings of tech executives in Washington. Nadella said he was focused on delivering results for the software company's customers. "I just don't want to be in Washington. I just want to be in Redmond, Washington," he joked, referring to the location of the company's headquarters. —Christina Cheddar Berk 43 Min Ago Jensen Huang exit from Nvidia is 'all sort of pretty tragic,' Microsoft's Nadella says Satya Nadella speaks onstage during the NY Times Dealbook Summit at Jazz at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Adam Gray | Getty Images The ouster of Jensen Huang after he acknowledged having extramarital relations, reportedly including an alleged Chinese spy, is "all sort of pretty tragic," Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the DealBook Summit. The two have known each other for many years. "I'm a great admirer of what he's done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out," Nadella said. "It's the Nvidia board's decision on what happens, but I'll just say this one thing, right? Knowing the team, you know, Colette sort of worked at Microsoft for a long time. I've known her for a long time. She's a tremendous person." Nadella, whose company relies on Nvidia graphics processing units for its artificial intelligence buildout, said he's in discussions with the same people he was before. He has run Microsoft since 2014 as the software maker's third CEO. The first was Bill Gates, a co-founder. Nadella himself is not a founder. Founders are "singular, but they're not gods, right?" Nadella said. The people who start companies don't live forever and do need to be eventually replaced, he said. "Singularity is about the magic you create, but it's also the institutional strength you build," Nadella said. "And so I think that's what Jensen actually has done with Nvidia." — Jordan Novet 53 Min Ago Microsoft CEO Nadella says he is 'extremely sorry' for extended Outlook outage Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks during the 2026 DealBook Summit in the Appel Room at Lincoln Center, Nov. 18, 2026 in New York City. Spencer Platt | Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was "extremely sorry" to those affected by the company's Outlook email software outage that played out over almost 24 hours last week. headlines.title: Retail investor enthusiasm for Anthropic IPO to rival SpaceX debut
headlines.summary: Anthropic is gearing up for a blockbuster initial public offering this week, and excitement among retail investors looks to be off the charts.
headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO: Retail investor demand boom Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Vanda Research estimates about $250 million of net retail buying on Anthropic’s first trading day, a forecast twice the size of the SpaceX IPO. Anthropic is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker ANT after plans to sell 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each. The bar for success is lower for Anthropic than SpaceX, as it comes at a time with the AI trade in turmoil. watch now VIDEO 7:59 07:59 Why retail investors are divided over Anthropic's IPO Markets and Politics Digital Original Video Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate. "I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said. Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO. "That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC. The artificial intelligence laboratory — which will trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol ANT — is selling 825 million shares at an expected price range of $70 to $78 per share in the IPO, though sources told CNBC the stock is likely to price above that range . Individual investors are expected to be allocated as much as 20% in that initial offering. And if Vanda's figures prove correct, the buying enthusiasm will be big as regular trading begins. Founded less than six years ago, Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving it a valuation of $1.405 trillion. If demand is especially strong, Anthropic could even raise more than the record $85.7 billion that SpaceX sold in its record IPO in June. The tech trade has been in turmoil since Jensen Huang's departure last week as Nvidia CEO raised questions about the future of AI financing. Before then, a potential slowdown in data center development resulting from Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, and signs of moderation in the capital expenditures boom, had already spooked investors. These all stand in marked contrast to the market backdrop in place at the time of the SpaceX IPO. In June, both positioning and sentiment were high, Malhi said. The Anthropic IPO could see a different dynamic, however. Demand could be strong across the entire investor spectrum given that sentiment is depressed, meaning that the bar to beat expectations is "much easier to overcome," he explained. "What we're seeing across both retail and institutional positioning is that there is plenty of dry powder to take part in this IPO," the strategist said. 'Pure-play AI leader' For the 27-year-old New Yorker Shetty, who himself works at agentic data platform Data Workers, this is his first time vying to take part in an IPO. He said Anthropic's emphasis on "safety first" drew his interest. "I've been telling all of my friends, 'If you have like $5, you should invest it in this stock because this is the pure-play AI leader,'" Shetty said. "I think of my father who invested in Microsoft during the dotcom bubble, and he divested from that stock, and it was such a silly thing to do." Not everyone agrees. Joe Pak, a former macro portfolio manager who is now an independent researcher outside London, is opting against participating in the Anthropic IPO for two reasons: the likelihood of limited allocation and current macroeconomic conditions. He believes the odds are probably stacked against retail investors when it comes to the allocation of shares. "It's very difficult as a retail investor to actually get an allocation in these blockbuster IPOs," the 36-year-old said. "You get maybe one share, and the base case is you don't get any at all. So, it's a bit of a catch-22. If you do get a lot of shares, it probably means that the institutional bid was weaker, and in that case, you don't actually want the shares at that level." In terms of the economy, conditions "need to be favorable" to hold a position in a stock like Anthropic, he said. But with the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September and widely expected to do so again next month, the backdrop could be darkening. "From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal. ... [But] it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor." Russ Faigen Retail investor "The risk that you have is the financial conditions deteriorating" before the company starts to grow into anticipated profit and revenue, which would justify purchase of the stock, Pak said. While Pak is steering clear of the IPO, he did say that at a certain level, it would make sense to get into Anthropic. Other retail investors such as Bryan Nearnberg share Pak's view. "I'm planning to eventually buy Anthropic, just not at the IPO price, considering when the lockups expire and there's some selling pressure," said the 37-year-old Westchester County, N.Y. resident, who works in finance operations. "We are not at the end of this short-term negative headline sentiment." IPOs are a sore spot for Nearnberg, who hasn't had much luck trading stocks on their opening day. His skepticism toward IPOs can be traced all the way back to when he was in college. "I didn't get an allocation to the Facebook IPO, but I ended up buying it the first day of open. I got burned pretty quickly," Nearnberg told CNBC. "Same thing with Zynga. I didn't get an allocation, but [got] burned pretty quickly in terms of price." As a result of those experiences, "I'm pretty sure we'll see a good entry price underneath the IPO for Anthropic by Memorial Day next year," Nearnberg said, citing sour sentiment toward technology and concern surrounding circular financing as short-term headwinds. Waiting game To be clear, all the retail investors CNBC spoke with are optimistic on AI as a transformative technology — even the ones sitting out the IPO. One trader said he believes in AI so much that he uses Anthropic's Claude, a conversational AI assistant, every day. But Russ Faigen, a 27-year-old in Austin, Texas, is undecided on whether to subscribe for a piece of the IPO. "From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal," Faigen said. But "it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor." Faigen, who works for an agentic brokerage firm, said he's "leaning towards patience," as he believes Anthropic is going to be public "for a very long time." "I just am not in a rush to get in on day one based off the valuation," he told CNBC. Anthropic's valuation depends on its ability to sustain its rapid growth. In the nine months through Sept. 30, revenue reached more than $33 billion, 1,200% above the year-earlier period. Aggregate spending commitments total about $900 billion , primarily centered around computing power and infrastructure. Breakneck growth leads plenty of retail and institutional investors to approach not just the Anthropic IPO but the entire AI trade with caution. "A lot of it comes down to scrutiny over how much money they're spending on AI," said Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro. "Investors want to see that those investments are turning into tangible returns, into tangible revenue." — CNBC's Charlotte Morabito contributed to this report Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and

headlines.article_text: Palo Alto Networks (PANW) Q1 2027 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palo Alto Networks topped Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates. The company is buying AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. Fears of AI-led attacks have fueled demand for Palo Alto's tools. In this article PANW Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:22 02:22 Palo Alto shares pop on Q1 revenue and earnings beat, raises full-year guidance Closing Bell: Overtime Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first quarter estimates and inked a deal for artificial intelligence startup Applied Compute . Here's how the company did versus LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : $1.05 adjusted vs. 97 cents expected Revenue : $3.44 billion vs $3.31 billion expected Revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter. Fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. Amid this backdrop, shares have jumped 85% this year. "As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely," CEO Nikesh Arora said in a release. Palo Alto said annual recurring revenue for its next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history. The cybersecurity company bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027 as business spend more on security in the age of AI. Palo Alto expects adjusted earnings per share in the range of $4.26 to 4.30 and revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to 14.57 billion. The forecasts topped the earnings of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue expected by analysts. Net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share, a year ago. Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI. Arora said the company's $4.5 billion all-stock deal for Applied Compute will help businesses secure open-weight models as adoption grows. The startup helps businesses run and customize their own AI models and marks a major investment for Palo Alto beyond cybersecurity. "If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on an earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do." Outages from Microsoft, banks and the FAA have heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week. U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity, but experts say the rapid acceleration in patching is straining dated systems. As businesses discover more vulnerabilities, Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year. "Whatever they do today is going to take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is," Arora said. Palo Alto Networks stock chart. headlines.article_text: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, above expected range, source tells CNBC Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, a person familiar told CNBC, above the expected range. The AI company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" on Thursday. Should the company sell all 825 million shares it had originally planned for the offering, the IPO will raise about $68.5 billion. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks during INBOUND 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center in San Francisco, Sept. 4, 2025. Chance Yeh | Getty Images Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, a person familiar told CNBC, above the expected range, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing and a historic moment for the artificial intelligence industry. The company previously said it was offering 825 million shares. If that number holds and all of shares are sold at the IPO price, Anthropic would raise roughly $68.5 billion. Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record, raising $75 billion initially and a total of $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment. Anthropic's market cap will depend on total shares outstanding, but the share price would put the valuation above the $1.4 trillion that Anthropic was previously targeting. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT." The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. After publicly unveiling its prospectus in October, Anthropic updated the document last week with an expected price range between $70 and $78 per share. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. What this analyst expects from the AI giant Anthropic IPO is not important anymore: 'Big Short' investor Steve Eisman Altimeter's Brad Gerstner aims to invest $5 billion in Anthropic IPO Anthropic IPO guide: Everything you need to know Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic Anthropic's Wall Street whisperer: CFO Krishna Rao "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time." Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."
